operationalization: Score milk-clotting gastric enzyme activity, or a chymosin ortholog as a proxy, across species with multi-chambered stomachs and in hares. The claim holds if both groups have it, and fails if a clear multi-chambered lineage or the hare lacks it.

candidate_datasets.name: UniProt
candidate_datasets.role: chymosin and related gastric aspartic proteases, as a molecular proxy for rennet across sequenced mammals

candidate_datasets.name: Ensembl
candidate_datasets.role: orthologs of the chymosin gene in ruminants, camelids, cetaceans and lagomorphs

obstacles: Multi-chambered stomachs occur in several unrelated groups, so the taxon set has to be defined before the enzyme is scored.
Gene presence is a proxy for the secreted rennet Aristotle meant, and hare data are sparse.
Lepus covers several species whose stomach biochemistry is not equally known.
rationale: Chymosin orthologs are openly listed for many mammals, which is enough to test a molecular proxy in the main ruminant lineages and in lagomorphs. Enzyme activity in the stomach, especially of the hare and of non-ruminant multi-chambered species such as cetaceans, still has to be compiled from physiological papers. That compilation can decide the named cases and leaves the universal quantifier only partly covered.

operationalization: Code reproductive mode as oviparous or internally brooded then live-bearing for Viperidae and for sharks and rays. The generalization holds only if both groups develop eggs internally and then bear live young; oviparous species in either group refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive mode of elasmobranchs, separating egg-laying from live-bearing after internal egg development

candidate_datasets.name: Sharkipedia
candidate_datasets.role: life-history traits for sharks and rays, including reproductive mode

candidate_datasets.name: The Reptile Database
candidate_datasets.role: species accounts for Viperidae stating whether a species lays eggs or bears live young

obstacles: Viperidae is mixed: some genera lay eggs, and Aristotle's viper may have been the European Vipera only.
Skates and some sharks lay egg cases, so the selachian universal is decidable and sensitive to how the group is bounded.
rationale: FishBase and Sharkipedia record reproductive mode for elasmobranchs in a form a small team can tabulate directly. Viper reproductive mode is stated in species accounts rather than one column, but the genera are few enough to compile in weeks. Together those sources can confirm or refute both halves of the generalization as a claim about the modern groups named in the scope.

operationalization: Score gallbladder presence and its attachment, liver versus intestine, across a phylogenetic sample of fishes. Universal presence fails if any major fish lineage lacks a gallbladder; the attachment clause fails if the liver is the usual site.

candidate_datasets.name: Phenoscape Knowledgebase
candidate_datasets.role: computable fish anatomical phenotypes from curated systematic matrices, where gallbladder characters were coded

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: anatomical accounts for exemplar fishes that mention the gallbladder and its position

obstacles: Attachment site is rarely a coded character, so most records speak only to presence.
Published matrices cover selected clades rather than fishes as a whole.
Aristotle's fishes include cartilaginous fishes, lampreys and bony fishes, which are not one anatomical sample.
rationale: Presence or absence of a gallbladder is a discrete anatomical character, and some fish matrices already code organ phenotypes. Coverage is a subset of clades, and the claim that the bladder is usually on the intestine rather than the liver is much thinner in those matrices. A team can test exemplar lineages now and would need a long compilation before the universal is settled.

operationalization: Record gallbladder presence or absence, and for the camel the presence of only small biliary vessels, in horse, mule, ass, deer, roe deer, camel, seals and dolphins. Each named case is confirmed by absence, or by reduced ducts in the camel, and refuted by a normal gallbladder.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: anatomical and natural-history accounts for the named ungulates, seals and dolphins

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: specimen media for the named species, useful where soft-tissue or contrast imaging shows the biliary tract

obstacles: The gallbladder is soft tissue and is often missing from skeletal scans, so accounts carry more weight than bone libraries.
Deer and seal each name a family, and a single species with a gallbladder would limit how far the group claim reaches.
rationale: The claim is a short list of presence, absence and duct reduction, and each named animal has a published visceral anatomy. A small team can score the list from species accounts and veterinary anatomy in days. Imaging repositories help where the biliary tract was actually scanned, and they are secondary to those accounts.

operationalization: Compare gallbladder presence and size in sheep and goats from Naxos with animals from the Chalcis district of Euboea, against the usual presence of a gallbladder in those species. The locality claim holds if Naxos animals are extreme and Euboean animals lack the organ.
obstacles: No public survey records gallbladder size or presence for sheep and goats by Greek locality.
Modern island breeds need a demonstrated link to the ancient stocks Aristotle named.
Routine slaughter statistics do not retain gallbladder measurements.
rationale: The variables are straightforward, presence and size by locality, and a dedicated survey could decide them. Nothing now in open trait databases or breed registries records gallbladder anatomy for Naxos versus Euboea. Existing livestock data identify breeds and places, and they omit the organ the claim is about.

operationalization: Regress size-corrected maximum longevity on gallbladder absence across mammals, with deer, horses, asses, camels and dolphins marked. The claim holds if absence predicts longer life after body size and phylogeny are accounted for, and fails if the association is flat or reversed.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: maximum longevity and adult body mass for mammals with and without a gallbladder

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: adult body mass and life-history covariates used to residualize longevity

obstacles: Gallbladder presence is not a column in the longevity databases and has to be compiled for the species that have longevity records.
Body size and phylogeny both predict lifespan, so an uncorrected comparison is uninformative.
Roe deer are short-lived for a 'deer' example, so the group label hides heterogeneity.
rationale: AnAge supplies the longevity side of the comparison for a large set of mammals, including the named kinds. The gallbladder character is real but scattered through anatomical sources, so only a subset of the longevity table can be scored quickly. Even on that subset, a clean result needs a phylogenetic model, which keeps the test informative and confounded.

operationalization: Score ink-sac presence across cuttlefish, squid and octopuses, and compare ink quantity or ink-sac volume scaled by body size, asking whether Sepia ranks highest. Universal presence fails if a cephalopod in that set lacks ink; the ranking fails if another genus stores more.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: species pages for cephalopods compiling published notes on the ink sac

candidate_datasets.name: MolluscaBase
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic frame for cuttlefish, squid and octopuses so ink records can be attached to names

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: accounts of ink use and the ink sac in common cephalopods

obstacles: Ink volume is described far more often than measured on a common scale.
Nautiluses lack an ink sac, so the result depends on whether 'all cephalopods' includes them or only Aristotle's coleoids.
rationale: Presence of an ink sac in the familiar coleoids is documented well enough to test that half of the claim from species accounts. A quantitative ranking of ink amount is not in any trait table, and the published measurements cover a handful of genera. The test can settle presence for the named kinds and only illustrate the 'most ink' ranking.

operationalization: Score a gastric mill, a second set of teeth in the stomach, in spiny lobsters, crayfish and crabs. The distributional claim holds if Carabi and only some crabs have one; the functional clause needs a further comparison of animals whose mouthparts already chew well.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: decapod species pages that summarize stomach anatomy where it has been published

candidate_datasets.name: World Register of Marine Species
candidate_datasets.role: name matching for Carabi, lobsters, crayfish and crabs

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: anatomical accounts of the decapod foregut and gastric mill

obstacles: Carabi maps uncertainly onto spiny lobsters, which lack chelae, and onto crayfish, which have them.
A gastric mill is widespread in decapods, so 'some crabs' needs an explicit species list.
Presence of the mill does not show that the mouthparts were insufficient.
rationale: The gastric mill is a standard decapod character and can be scored for the main groups from carcinological descriptions. Name matching for Carabi changes which animals enter the test, and the 'because' clause is a functional claim that presence data leave open. Existing accounts can test the anatomical distribution on a restricted set of families.

operationalization: Track gonad index across the lunar month in Mediterranean edible sea urchins, with nighttime sea temperature and feeding rate as covariates. The size claim holds if gonads peak at full moon; the warmth explanation holds only if temperature, rather than feeding, accounts for that peak.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive notes for echinoids, including lunar spawning where a species page records it

candidate_datasets.name: World Echinoidea Database
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic frame for the edible sea-urchin species in Aristotle's scope

obstacles: Lunar gonad series exist for some tropical species and are sparse for the Mediterranean species he would have seen.
Moonlight does not supply a sea-temperature treatment, and tides, spawning cycles and feeding move together.
No open dataset holds gonad index, intake and temperature on the same lunar calendar.
rationale: A lunar peak in gonad size is measurable and has been published for particular urchins, so a subset of the pattern can be reviewed now. Those series rarely pair feeding and nighttime temperature with gonad size, which is what would separate Aristotle's warmth explanation from a feeding explanation. The mechanism half of the claim stays out of reach of the existing tables.

operationalization: Count gonads ('eggs'), lantern teeth and stomach compartments across regular and irregular echinoids. The claim holds if every sea urchin has five of each; any order with a different gonad count or without a lantern refutes the universal.

candidate_datasets.name: World Echinoidea Database
candidate_datasets.role: classification of regular and irregular echinoids whose diagnoses state lantern and gonad patterns

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: scans and photographs of tests and lanterns from which tooth count can be scored

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: anatomical accounts of Aristotle's lantern, gonads and gut compartments in sea urchins

obstacles: Aristotle's eggs are gonads and his stomachs are the five pouches around the lantern, so the counts have to follow that anatomy.
Irregular echinoids often reduce the lantern and the gonad number, and skeletal repositories show teeth more readily than gonads.
rationale: Five-part organization of regular sea urchins is standard morphology and can be checked from diagnoses, accounts and lantern specimens. Irregular groups are in the same taxonomic database and are the natural refuting cases if 'all sea urchins' is taken at face value. Gonad counts are soft-tissue records, and order-level descriptions already state them well enough for a decision.

operationalization: The passage asserts an unbroken natural scale from lifeless things through plant-like beings to animals, with neighbours scarcely different. No measurement of disparity or of phylogenetic distance supplies a threshold that would confirm or refute that picture without replacing it.
obstacles: 'Unbroken sequence' and 'scarcely any difference' have no decision criterion.
A tree, a life-versus-nonlife boundary, or a disparity statistic would test a modern stand-in for the claim.
rationale: This is a statement about how nature is arranged, not a comparative measurement with a confirming and a refuting result. Phenotypic and phylogenetic datasets can describe gaps and clusters, and any degree of similarity can still be called a close approach. The claim therefore has no empirical resolution that preserves what it says.

operationalization: Identify the food of adult cicadas by gut contents, feeding traces or stable isotopes. The claim holds if atmospheric moisture accounts for their intake, and fails if they feed on plant sap.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biotic Interactions (GloBI)
candidate_datasets.role: species-interaction records linking cicadas to food plants where those records exist

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: feeding accounts for Cicadidae, including xylem feeding versus dew

obstacles: GloBI's coverage of cicadas is incomplete, so species accounts still have to be read.
Occasional dew drinking can sit alongside sap feeding, and the claim requires moisture from the air as the food.
The aside that insects eat little because they are cold is a separate, non-measured explanation.
rationale: Cicada diet is a standard natural-history variable, documented in accounts and in interaction records that point to plants. A small team can score the family well enough to decide whether air-deposited moisture is their food. The cold-nature gloss does not add a second observable beyond that diet.

operationalization: Compare wing count, two versus four, with body size across flying insects, treating flies and bees as the named anchors. The claim holds if a small size class has two wings and larger fliers have four, and fails if tiny four-winged insects or large two-winged insects are common.

candidate_datasets.name: Integrated Taxonomic Information System
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic frame for insect orders whose wing counts are stable, to be joined to body-size records

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: exemplar accounts stating wing number for flies, bees and other flying insects

obstacles: No open table pairs wing count with body size across insects.
'Very small' has no stated cutoff.
Minute wasps have four wings and large flies have two, so order-level proxies answer a different question from the size rule.
rationale: Wing number is discrete and, for exemplar orders, already written in ordinary descriptions, so counterexamples can be assembled. A fair test of 'very small implies two wings' needs a size-stratified sample that does not exist as a dataset. Existing sources can refute a crude version on well-known orders and cannot yet carry a quantitative rule for flying insects as a whole.

operationalization: Measure the frequency of a larger right claw in crabs, in Carabi, and in clawed lobsters. 'Invariably' requires a right-claw bias indistinguishable from all individuals; the lobster clause holds if side is about even.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: decapod accounts that report claw asymmetry where it has been studied

candidate_datasets.name: World Register of Marine Species
candidate_datasets.role: matching of Carabi, crabs and lobsters to modern families

obstacles: Carabi is an unstable name, and spiny lobsters do not have crushing claws.
Laterality frequencies are published for a few crabs and for Homarus, not for crabs as a class.
A single left-handed individual refutes 'invariably' if that word is taken literally.
rationale: Claw laterality is measurable and already counted in papers on shore crabs and the European lobster. Those studies cover a small slice of the groups named, and the identity of Carabi changes the hypothesis. The existing counts can test a few genera and leave the universal over crabs unresolved.

operationalization: Count arms in cuttlefish, squid and octopuses, and compare arm length scaled by mantle length. The claim holds if all three have eight arms and the arms are short in cuttlefish and squid and longer in octopuses.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: cephalopod species pages describing arm and tentacle counts and relative arm length

candidate_datasets.name: MolluscaBase
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic frame for Sepia, teuthids and octopods

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: anatomical accounts of arm number and proportion in the common genera

obstacles: Squid and cuttlefish also have two tentacles, which must be kept distinct from the eight arms.
Relative length is often qualitative in accounts.
Nautiluses fall outside the eight-arm pattern if the claim is read as all cephalopods.
rationale: Arm counts for the three groups Aristotle compares are standard and repeated in public species accounts. Relative length is described consistently enough, even without a morphometric table, for a small team to score the contrast he draws. Extending the same count to nautiluses is a boundary choice, and within the stated scope the comparison is decidable.

operationalization: Count cervical vertebrae, and any fusion into one element, in wolves and lions, and compare that count with other mammals that have a neck. The claim holds only if the wolf and lion neck is a single bone.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: skeletal scans of Canis lupus and Panthera leo from which cervical counts can be taken

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: digital cranial and cervical anatomy of mammals, including large carnivores where digitized

candidate_datasets.name: VertNet
candidate_datasets.role: museum skeletal specimens of wolves and lions with vertebral series

obstacles: Cervical count is scored from specimens or accounts rather than a precomputed longevity-style column.
The named species are the whole scope, and both are well represented in collections.
rationale: A single neck bone versus several vertebrae is directly visible on skeletons, and wolves and lions are in open morphology repositories and museum indexes. Scoring a few specimens decides the claim. The same collections supply the comparison with other necked mammals.

operationalization: Compare withers height of foals with adult withers height, and test whether the hind hoof reaches the head in foals and fails to do so in adults. The claim holds if young solid-hoofed and cloven-hoofed animals are nearly adult in height because the limbs are disproportionately long.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: juvenile and adult limb elements of horses and other ungulates for relative leg length

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: growth and proportion notes for horses and other hoofed mammals

obstacles: Withers-height series live in husbandry papers rather than one open growth table.
The hind-hoof-to-head movement is a flexibility observation and is rarely measured.
The claim also covers cloven-hoofed quadrupeds, which are less completely measured than the horse.
rationale: Relative limb length of young versus adult ungulates can be approached with museum specimens and with published horse growth curves. Those sources cover the horse better than the whole hoofed scope, and they rarely record the reaching movement. The height comparison is partly testable now; the behavioral clause is thinly documented.

operationalization: The claim assigns hands to humans because they are intelligent enough to use them. Co-occurrence of hands and intelligence does not separate that final-cause order from the opposite story, and a phylogenetic sequence of dexterity and brain size would be a different claim.
obstacles: No observation distinguishes nature's assigning hands for the sake of intelligence from the bare conjunction of the two traits.
Replacing the final cause with an evolutionary order changes the claim.
rationale: This is a teleological ranking of causes. Human hands and human intelligence are both observable, and nothing in existing data says which exists for the sake of the other. The passage is therefore not empirically resolvable on its own terms.

operationalization: Count digits, including the dewclaw, on each forefoot and hind foot of wolves, lions, dogs and leopards. The claim holds if forefeet have five digits and hind feet have four.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: pedal skeletons of the named carnivores

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: digit anatomy for mammal specimens that have been digitized

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: toe-count statements in species accounts for canids and felids

obstacles: Domestic dogs often carry a hind dewclaw, so 'dogs' is not a single count.
The forelimb dewclaw is a reduced digit and has to be included on purpose.
rationale: Digit number in these four carnivores is elementary anatomy and is visible on skeletons and written in species accounts. A small team can score the named species, and the dog dewclaw is the main within-group complication. The claim as restricted to these animals is decidable with current specimens and accounts.

operationalization: Pair teat number and position, inguinal versus abdominal, with litter size across viviparous quadrupeds. The claim holds if animals with small litters have two inguinal teats and litter-bearers have many teats along the belly.

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: litter size and adult body mass for mammals

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: litter size and reproductive traits for the named ungulates and carnivores

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: teat number and position in species accounts for horse, camel, deer, ox, goat, pig, dog and lion

obstacles: Teat number and position are not columns in the life-history tables and have to be compiled.
Shared ancestry tracks both litter size and teat pattern.
Primates, with two pectoral teats and usually one young, sit outside the thigh-versus-belly wording.
rationale: Litter size for the relevant mammals is in open life-history databases, and teat counts for the familiar livestock and carnivores are in species accounts. Joining the two for a phylogenetic test is a real compilation, feasible for the named species and incomplete for viviparous quadrupeds at large. The data can test the stated examples and a partial comparative version of the rule.

operationalization: Record the direction of the urine stream, rearward versus forward or lateral, in female quadrupeds, in lynx, lion, camel and hare males, and in solid-hoofed males. The universals hold only if every female and no solid-hoofed animal directs urine backward, with the named males as the male exceptions.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: elimination and urogenital notes for the named genera

obstacles: 'Backwards' has no standard angular criterion.
Quantitative records exist for a few domestic and zoo species, while most quadrupeds are undescribed on this point.
The orientation of the urethral opening is an anatomical proxy for the behavior.
rationale: Direction of urination is observable and is described for horses, camels, lions and a few other familiar species. Those accounts can speak to the named exceptions and to solid-hoofed animals. They do not cover female quadrupeds as a class, so the universal remains untested.

operationalization: Score external tail presence and a distinct buttock, a fleshy gluteal mass used in upright posture, in humans and in quadrupeds. The anatomical claim holds if humans lack a tail and quadrupeds lack buttocks; the nourishment story has no separate measurement.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: caudal regions and pelves of humans and quadrupeds

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: tail and locomotor descriptions across mammals, including apes

obstacles: A buttock is a soft-tissue shape, whereas skeletal collections show caudal vertebrae.
Many mammals lack an external tail, so 'man alone' is a broad comparative claim.
Diversion of tail nourishment into the buttocks yields no distinct observation.
rationale: Tail reduction and pelvic form can be compared with skeletons and species accounts, which is enough to test whether tail loss and buttocks are uniquely human. The nutritional explanation of that pattern does not differ observationally from the anatomy itself. The result is a partial test of the anatomical clauses.

operationalization: Score a huckle-bone as the double-pulley astragalus, and tabulate it against polydactyl, solid-hoofed and cloven-hoofed feet. The claim holds if polydactyl quadrupeds lack that bone, solid-hoofed animals usually lack it, and the animals that have it are mostly cloven-hoofed.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: ankle skeletons across artiodactyls, perissodactyls and multi-toed mammals

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: astragalus morphology for digitized mammal specimens

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: foot-type and ankle descriptions for the main ungulate and carnivore groups

obstacles: Every tetrapod has a talus; the claim is about the dice-shaped artiodactyl astragalus.
Foot categories have to be applied the same way to each specimen.
rationale: The double-trochlea astragalus is a standard osteological character and is visible in open skeletal collections. Foot type is likewise standard. A small team can cross-tabulate the two across living quadruped orders and decide the generalization.

operationalization: Score tongue presence in the Nile crocodile and in other oviparous quadrupeds and snakes. The claim holds if every such animal has a tongue except the river crocodile, which has only an empty space.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: oral-cavity accounts for crocodilians, lizards, turtles and snakes

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: head specimens of Crocodylus niloticus, informative where soft tissue is preserved

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: cranial anatomy of crocodilians and other reptiles

obstacles: The crocodile tongue is soft tissue and is easy to miss on a dry skull.
A tongue that is present and immobile still counts as a tongue under a presence criterion.
rationale: Tongue presence in reptiles is ordinary anatomy and is stated in species accounts for crocodilians, lizards, turtles and snakes. The river crocodile is the single exception the claim needs, and it is well described. Skeletal scans are supplementary because the character is soft tissue.

operationalization: Score which eyelid closes the eye in lizards, turtles, crocodilians and birds. The claim holds if these animals lack a functional upper eyelid and close the eye with the lower lid.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: eye and eyelid descriptions for lepidosaurs, turtles, crocodilians and birds

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: orbital anatomy for reptile specimens where the lids can be interpreted

obstacles: Snakes have a spectacle rather than mobile lids.
Crocodilians, geckos and birds differ from typical lizards in how the upper lid and the nictitating membrane work.
Family-level scoring still has to be compiled from descriptions.
rationale: Eyelid mechanics are described at the level of the major groups the claim covers, and those descriptions are public. A small team can score lizards, turtles, crocodilians and birds as groups and decide whether lower-lid closure is general. Within-group exceptions are part of that same literature, so they narrow the claim rather than leaving it untestable.

operationalization: In the Nile crocodile, measure which element rotates at the jaw joint relative to the braincase, and separately how the head moves relative to the ground during a bite. The claim holds if the upper jaw is the element that moves on the skull; movement of the head on the neck is a different result.

candidate_datasets.name: DigiMorph
candidate_datasets.role: cranial and jaw-joint models of crocodilians

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: skulls of Crocodylus showing the jaw articulation

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: functional accounts of crocodile feeding and jaw movement

obstacles: Relative to the skull the mandible is the mobile element; relative to the ground the whole head lifts.
Published kinematic series cover few individuals.
Aristotle's observation matches the head-lifting frame, so the criterion has to be stated before the data decide anything.
rationale: The jaw joint itself is visible on specimens and is enough to say which bone articulates. Feeding kinematics that would match Aristotle's frame, the head rising while the lower jaw stays near the substrate, exist for a few animals and are not a systematic dataset. The anatomical test is feasible, and the reference frame keeps it from being a clean decision.

operationalization: Score milk or mammary glands against reproductive mode. The claim holds if milk and mammae occur only in internally viviparous animals, and fails if any egg-laying or otherwise non-internally-viviparous animal lactates.

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: mammal species list and life history, including monotremes and therian mammals

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive mode and longevity records that identify monotremes, marsupials and placentals

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: lactation and reproductive-mode accounts, including monotremes and birds that produce crop secretions

obstacles: Monotremes lay eggs and lactate, so they are the decisive case and must be inside the taxon set.
Pigeon crop milk is a different secretion and has to be kept outside mammary milk by the definition used.
rationale: Reproductive mode and lactation are both standard, and monotremes are present in mammal life-history databases and species accounts. A small team can ask whether any non-internally-viviparous animal has milk. That comparison decides the universal as stated.

operationalization: Correlate neck length with leg length across birds, coding webbed feet as the stated exception. The claim holds if neck and leg lengths track each other once web-footed birds are set aside, and if those web-footed birds break the pattern.

candidate_datasets.name: AVONET
candidate_datasets.role: tarsus length, wing and mass for birds, covering the leg side of the comparison; neck length is not a column

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: bird skeletons from which neck length can be measured for a sample

candidate_datasets.name: Birds of the World
candidate_datasets.role: species accounts describing neck, leg and foot type, including webbed feet

obstacles: Neck length is absent from the main open avian morphometric table.
Web-footed birds range from long-necked swans to short-necked auks, so the exception class is heterogeneous.
A phylogenetic model is required before the correlation can be read as a rule.
rationale: Leg length and foot type are available for essentially all birds, and neck length can be measured on a skeletal sample or taken from accounts for a subset. That is enough to test the rule in part. A full-scope test waits on a neck-length compilation joined to the existing leg data.

operationalization: Code tarsal or wing spurs and predatory talons as two binary traits across birds. The co-occurrence claim holds if no species has both; the remark that nature makes nothing superfluous has no further observation.

candidate_datasets.name: Birds of the World
candidate_datasets.role: species accounts describing spurs, claws and feet for galliforms, jacanas, screamers and raptors

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: foot descriptions for exemplar gamebirds and birds of prey

obstacles: Spur and talon need explicit definitions before a species is scored.
Full species accounts are partly paywalled.
The final-cause sentence is not a separate measurable claim.
rationale: Spurs and talons are described in standard bird accounts, and the relevant groups are few enough that a team can search them. There is no open character column for either trait, so the work is a compilation rather than a download. The mutual-exclusion clause can be tested on a well-defined subset; the teleological gloss cannot.

operationalization: Count toes on each foot across birds, with the ostrich set aside as the claim allows. The claim holds if every other bird has four toes.

candidate_datasets.name: Birds of the World
candidate_datasets.role: toe counts in species accounts across bird families

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: foot descriptions for ratites, shorebirds, woodpeckers and other groups that vary in toe number

obstacles: Toe number is written in descriptions rather than in the AVONET measurement table.
Three-toed ratites, some shorebirds and some woodpeckers remain inside the claim once the ostrich is excluded.
rationale: Toe count is a discrete, universally described bird character. Setting the ostrich aside is explicit in the claim, and the remaining families can be scored from handbooks and accounts in weeks. Exceptions outside the ostrich decide the universal.

operationalization: Code toe arrangement as two-forward-two-back versus three-forward-one-back for the wryneck and for other birds. The claim holds only if Jynx is the sole two-and-two species.

candidate_datasets.name: Birds of the World
candidate_datasets.role: toe arrangement for wrynecks, other woodpeckers, parrots, cuckoos, toucans and trogons

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: zygodactyl and heterodactyl foot descriptions for the main bird groups

obstacles: Zygodactyly, heterodactyly and a reversible outer toe have to be distinguished.
Woodpeckers other than the wryneck are the closest comparison, and parrots and cuckoos are further two-and-two cases.
rationale: Foot arrangement is standard in bird descriptions, and the wryneck's identity is unambiguous. A small team can list the other two-and-two and two-back arrangements from family accounts. That list decides whether the wryneck is unique.

operationalization: Count paired pectoral and pelvic fins, which are the four fins in this passage, across fishes, treating broad flat batoids as the stated exception. The claim holds if non-flat fishes have four and no fish has more than four.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: pectoral and pelvic fin fields, from which paired-fin presence and counts can be taken

obstacles: Median fins are outside the four Aristotle is counting.
A blank fin-ray field has to be separated from a genuinely absent pelvic fin.
Eels and other non-flat fishes often lack pelvic fins, which bears on the 'have four' clause.
rationale: FishBase records paired-fin rays for a very large fraction of fish species and can be downloaded and scored with ordinary filters. The maximum of four paired fins and the claim that non-flat fishes have all four are both decidable from those fields. Batoids are identifiable in the same table and can be set aside as the text does.

operationalization: Score an operculum against skeleton type for elasmobranchs, chimaeras, sturgeons and bony fishes. The distributional claim holds if selachians lack gill covers; the 'because cartilage' clause holds only if cartilaginous-skeleton fishes in general lack them.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: classification of cartilaginous and bony fishes, with gill-cover details in the morphology sections of bony fishes

candidate_datasets.name: World Register of Marine Species
candidate_datasets.role: taxon matching for selachians, chimaeras and chondrosteans

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: gill-slit and operculum descriptions for sharks, rays, chimaeras and sturgeons

obstacles: Chimaeras have a soft opercular flap on a cartilaginous skeleton.
Sturgeons have an operculum and a largely cartilaginous skeleton, which is the comparison that bears on the causal clause.
rationale: Operculum presence is a group-level character already reflected in fish databases and in elasmobranch trait compilations. The selachian half can be read off directly. The causal half is decided by the same character in other cartilaginous-skeleton fishes, which are in the same taxonomic systems.

operationalization: Code mouth position as ventral versus terminal in dolphins and in selachians, and code whether feeding requires rolling onto the back. The claim holds if both groups have an underslung mouth and turn over to eat.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: mouth position for sharks and rays

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: dolphin and whale species pages describing mouth position and feeding posture

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: feeding accounts for dolphins and for sharks that roll or do not roll while taking prey

obstacles: Dolphin mouths are described as terminal on the beak, so the cetacean half may not match the shark coding.
Belly-up feeding is a behavior and is not a FishBase field.
Many sharks feed without rolling over, so mouth position alone does not establish the posture clause.
rationale: Mouth position for sharks and rays is a coded morphological field and can be tested now. The turning-over clause, and the inclusion of dolphins, depend on behavioral and anatomical accounts that cover common species and leave most selachians undescribed. The claim is decidable in part.

operationalization: Score sperm-producing testes, external or internal, in fishes and in snakes and other footless vertebrates. The claim holds only if those animals lack testes and have only sperm ducts.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive biology of fishes; male gonads are described in species summaries and the anatomical literature rather than a single presence column

candidate_datasets.name: The Reptile Database
candidate_datasets.role: snake species accounts and anatomical literature pointers for male reproductive organs

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: testis descriptions for fishes and snakes

obstacles: Aristotle treated elongate gonads as ducts, so the criterion has to be a sperm-producing organ rather than a compact scrotal testis.
Footless animals include caecilians and eels as well as snakes, and coverage is best for fishes and snakes.
rationale: Male gonads of fishes and snakes are described throughout comparative anatomy and are reflected in reproductive sections of public databases and accounts. A presence criterion decides the universal. The duct-versus-testis wording is a relabeling that the histology and gross anatomy can still address, because the organs produce sperm.

operationalization: Test whether the cetacean blowhole is connected to water taken in by the mouth, using airway-versus-esophagus anatomy and the composition of the blow. The claim holds if expelled water is swallowed seawater, and fails if the blow is respiratory vapor from a separate airway.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: respiratory and feeding anatomy of dolphins and whales, including the blowhole and the separation from the mouth

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: cetacean species pages summarizing the blowhole and lung

obstacles: The decisive anatomy is in descriptions rather than a trait column.
Chemical samples of the blow exist for a few species.
The claim covers dolphins, porpoises and whales, and the common species are the ones with detailed anatomy.
rationale: The connection between mouth, lungs and blowhole is established anatomy for the cetaceans the claim names, and it is written in public species accounts. That anatomy decides whether the blowhole vents swallowed seawater. Direct assays of blow composition add a second line of evidence for a smaller set of species.

operationalization: The claim says nature avoids the infinite because the infinite is incomplete, and therefore seeks an end. No dataset distinguishes that principle from any particular finite life cycle.
obstacles: 'Avoids the infinite' and 'seeks an end' state no confirming or refuting observation.
The application to spontaneous generation, that new kinds do not form an endless series, is a different and narrower claim.
rationale: This is a metaphysical constraint on nature. Finite generation, extinction and bounded clutch sizes are all compatible with it, and so are their opposites if one redescribes the end nature is said to seek. The sentence has no empirical decision criterion.

operationalization: Score sexual system, separate sexes versus hermaphroditism versus no gametes, in sessile shelled molluscs and in attached animals such as barnacles, sponges and ascidians. Separate males and females refute a claim of no sexes; hermaphroditism matches his plant comparison only under that reading.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive mode for bivalves, gastropods, barnacles, sponges and ascidians where pages record it

candidate_datasets.name: MolluscaBase
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic frame for testaceans as shelled molluscs

candidate_datasets.name: World Register of Marine Species
candidate_datasets.role: names and higher classification for attached marine animals in the scope

obstacles: Testaceans map to a mixed set of shelled molluscs, and attached animals add further phyla.
Hermaphroditism can be scored either as combined sexes or as the 'no sex' condition he attributes to plants.
Many bivalves have separate sexes, which is the clearest opposing outcome.
rationale: Sexual systems of common bivalves, snails, barnacles and ascidians are in marine species compilations and in the taxonomic literature those compilations summarize. Coverage is good for commercial and coastal genera and thin elsewhere. The test can decide the claim for those genera once hermaphroditism is given an explicit reading.

operationalization: The claim assigns the efficient cause of generation to the male and the material cause to the female. Those are Aristotelian causal roles, and an observation that the egg contributes cytoplasm or that the sperm contributes a genome replaces the claim with a different one.
obstacles: Efficient cause and material cause are not measurements.
Embryological and genetic datasets become relevant only after the four causes are translated away.
rationale: The sentence states a principle of explanation. Modern reproductive data describe contributions of egg and sperm in chemical and genetic terms, which do not confirm or refute 'efficient' versus 'material' as he uses those words. The claim stays conceptual.

operationalization: Compare sexually dimorphic traits before and after castration in males, asking whether most of them move to the female mean. The claim holds if the whole form shifts toward the female, and fails if only a few traits change or the animal remains clearly male in overall form.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: notes on secondary sexual characters, including antlers and other traits known to depend on the testes, for exemplar species

obstacles: 'Nearly the whole form' and 'seems female' need a declared trait list and a distance.
Published castration effects are concentrated on livestock, deer, horses and a few birds.
Age and breed confound before-after comparisons.
rationale: Effects of castration on particular dimorphic characters are documented for domestic animals and deer, so a partial test is possible from that literature. There is no cross-species table of whole-form change. The strong wording, that the animal becomes female or nearly so in form, can be assessed only for those well-studied species.

operationalization: Score testes versus sperm ducts alone in fishes and snakes. The claim holds if males of both groups lack testes and possess only two spermatic ducts.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive biology of fishes; testis anatomy is in species summaries and standard comparative anatomy

candidate_datasets.name: The Reptile Database
candidate_datasets.role: snake accounts pointing to internal male reproductive organs

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: testis descriptions for fishes and serpents

obstacles: Elongate gonads are the structures Aristotle called ducts; the decision criterion is whether those structures are testes.
Coverage is broad for fishes and adequate at family level for snakes.
rationale: The same anatomical sources that describe fish and snake reproduction identify paired male gonads. That identification decides a claim of absence. Compiling the score from databases and standard accounts is ordinary work for a small team.

operationalization: Record whether testes are internal and lie near the kidneys in birds and in oviparous quadrupeds such as lizards, turtles and crocodiles. The claim holds if both location conditions are general in those groups.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: urogenital anatomy for birds, lizards, turtles and crocodilians

candidate_datasets.name: The Reptile Database
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic and account coverage for oviparous reptiles

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: species lists and life history confirming which birds and reptiles fall in the scope

obstacles: 'Near the loin, by the kidneys' is a position claim, not mere absence of a scrotum.
Species accounts mention position unevenly, while group-level anatomy is consistent.
rationale: Internal testes beside the kidneys are group-level characters for birds and for the oviparous reptiles Aristotle includes. Public accounts state them, and the groups themselves are listed in life-history and taxonomic databases. A small team can score the groups and decide the generalization.

operationalization: Score the uterus or its analogue as paired or single across females, including mammals, birds and the invertebrate groups in the surrounding discussion. The claim holds if the organ is always double in the same sense that testes are two.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: uterus and oviduct descriptions for mammals, birds and other vertebrates

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: mammal species for which uterine type can be joined from anatomical accounts

obstacles: 'Double' can mean two horns, two oviducts or two chambers, and a simplex uterus is a fused pair.
Most birds have one functional oviduct.
Crustacean, cephalopod and insect gonoducts are a further mapping.
rationale: Uterine form is well described for mammals and birds, so those classes can be scored from accounts, with life-history lists supplying the species frame. The word 'always' reaches invertebrates whose paired ducts are described unevenly, and the criterion of doubling is itself ambiguous. The vertebrate portion is testable; the full universal is only partly so.

operationalization: Compare copulation duration of fishes, snakes, birds and oviparous quadrupeds with that of mammals that have external testes. The claim holds if every internal-testis or duct-only species is faster than the external-testis species.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: mating descriptions that sometimes give copulation duration for exemplar vertebrates

obstacles: Duration data are scattered through behavioral papers and cover a biased subset of species.
Some snakes with internal testes mate for hours, which is a serious confound for a simple ranking.
Mating system and body size track duration along with testis position.
rationale: Copulation duration is measurable and published for many vertebrates, including both internal-testis and scrotal species. There is no open comparative table, and the studies that exist are enough to inspect a biased sample rather than to rank all of the groups. Phylogeny and mating system keep even that sample from being a clean test.

operationalization: Compare testis mass in the breeding season with testis mass afterward for seasonally pairing birds. The claim holds if testes enlarge sharply at copulation and then shrink to near invisibility.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: breeding-season summaries for birds, with testis-cycle notes where accounts include them

candidate_datasets.name: Amniote life-history database
candidate_datasets.role: life-history timing for birds, including clutches per year and age at maturity, as context for published seasonal testis series

obstacles: Testis-volume series sit in avian endocrinology papers rather than one repository.
Year-round breeders are outside the seasonal clause.
'Almost indiscernible' needs a size threshold.
rationale: Seasonal growth and regression of bird testes is a repeatedly measured variable, especially in temperate passerines and in poultry. A team can compile those series for a solid subset of seasonal breeders. A dataset that already holds testis size for birds at large does not exist, so the full scope stays partial.

operationalization: Record mating posture in Erinaceus, upright and face to face versus a posterior mount, and relate that posture to the spines. The posture claim holds if they copulate standing upright; a posterior mount with lowered spines fails it.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive-behavior account for the European hedgehog

obstacles: Posture is described in natural-history narratives and films, not in a measurement archive.
The spine explanation is settled only once the posture itself is known.
Other hedgehog genera are poorly described compared with Erinaceus europaeus.
rationale: The European hedgehog's mating posture is described in public natural-history accounts, which is enough to examine the upright-stance claim for that species. The records are few and qualitative. Other hedgehogs, and a measured link between spine length and posture, are much thinner.

operationalization: Code whether cartilaginous fishes and vipers form eggs internally and then bear live young. The claim holds for a group only if that two-step mode is general in it.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: elasmobranch reproductive mode

candidate_datasets.name: Sharkipedia
candidate_datasets.role: shark and ray reproductive mode as a trait

candidate_datasets.name: The Reptile Database
candidate_datasets.role: Viperidae accounts stating egg-laying versus live birth

obstacles: Oviparous skates, catsharks and some viper genera decide the universals if the groups are taken at modern scope.
Yolk-sac and placental live birth both begin with an internal egg, which matches the wording if the egg stage is real.
rationale: This is the same reproductive-mode comparison as the Parts of Animals passage on vipers and selachians, and the same open sources cover it. Elasmobranch mode is tabulated; viper mode is in species accounts that can be compiled quickly. The generalization can be confirmed or refuted for both groups.

operationalization: Compare body temperature and egg-covering rigidity of live-bearing sharks and vipers with their egg-laying relatives. The cold-nature explanation holds if the live-bearers are colder and their coverings are soft because of that cold.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: preferred temperature and reproductive mode for sharks and rays

candidate_datasets.name: Sharkipedia
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive mode of sharks and rays, to be set beside FishBase temperature fields

obstacles: 'Cold nature' is not a body-temperature measurement.
Regionally warm-bodied sharks that bear live young cut against a cold-cause story.
Eggshell thickness and maternal temperature are rarely measured in the same study.
rationale: Temperature preferences and reproductive mode can be joined for many sharks, which tests a thermal proxy for 'cold nature'. Viper body temperatures and the softness of their egg coverings are scattered, and a temperature difference would still leave the causal story confounded with phylogeny. The data support a partial, proxy test.

operationalization: Locate the testes of elephants and hedgehogs as scrotal or internal. The location claim holds if both are internal; the claim that their skin cannot form a scrotum is not decided by location alone.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: male reproductive anatomy of elephants and hedgehogs

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: abdominal scans or dissections, where soft tissue shows testis position

obstacles: Testis position is documented in accounts; skin suitability is a functional gloss.
Skeletal repositories often omit the soft-tissue location.
Other testicond mammals show that internal testes occur with more than one skin type.
rationale: Internal testes in the elephant and the hedgehog are standard mammalogy and are stated in species accounts, so the location half can be decided now. The explanation from unsuitable skin does not make a prediction that location data can separate from other reasons for testicondy. The claim is only partly resolvable.

operationalization: Code mating posture in octopuses, cuttlefish and squid as mouth-to-mouth with intertwined arms, or as some other approach. The claim holds if that posture is the cephalopod mode.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive-behavior notes for common cephalopods

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: mating descriptions for octopus, cuttlefish and squid

obstacles: The three groups do not mate in one posture.
Many species have never been seen mating, so published observations are biased toward coastal genera.
Insertion of an arm into the mantle can co-occur with a head-to-head approach.
rationale: Mating has been described for the common octopus, cuttlefish and several squids, and those descriptions are summarized in public accounts. They can test the posture claim for those genera. They do not establish a single mode for cephalopods, and unobserved species remain a large share of the group.

operationalization: Examine the octopus arm that enters the female's funnel for a sperm groove or spermatophores, and for a connection to the male's seminal passage. The claim holds if that arm is only a holdfast and carries no generative role.

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: notes on the hectocotylus and spermatophore transfer in octopuses

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: anatomical accounts of the specialized octopus arm

candidate_datasets.name: MolluscaBase
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic frame for Octopus and related genera with a hectocotylus

obstacles: The spermatophore groove is described for common species and is not a filled column for every octopus.
Aristotle's poulp is the common octopus and its relatives, which are the best-described cases.
rationale: The specialized arm and its role in passing spermatophores are described in detail for the octopuses Aristotle would have meant, and those descriptions are public. Anatomy that shows sperm on the arm, or a groove continuous with the male system, decides whether the arm is outside generation. A small team can score the well-known species and settle the claim as he framed it.

operationalization: Trace life cycles of fleas, flies and blister beetles from egg to adult, and ask whether adults appear from putrefying matter with no parents. The claim holds only if those insects arise without conspecific parents and, when they do unite, fail to produce their own kind.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: life-cycle accounts for fleas, flies and blister beetles

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biotic Interactions (GloBI)
candidate_datasets.role: interaction records tying these insects to hosts, dung or carrion, as context for where eggs are laid

candidate_datasets.name: Integrated Taxonomic Information System
candidate_datasets.role: name matching for Siphonaptera, Diptera and Meloidae, including cantharides

obstacles: Cantharides maps to blister beetles, whose parasitic larval stages are easy to confuse with generation from carrion.
Flies lay eggs on putrefying matter, so substrate and parentage have to be scored separately.
Complete life cycles are in handbooks rather than one life-cycle table.
rationale: The life cycles of fleas, flies and blister beetles are fully described in public entomology, including the eggs and the role of rotting substrates. Those accounts decide whether the animals arise from putrefaction without parents. The work is compilation of known cycles, not a search for missing data.

operationalization: Estimate the proportion of copulating insect species in which female body length exceeds male body length. The claim holds if that proportion is a majority under a stated species universe.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: body-size and sex notes for exemplar insect orders

candidate_datasets.name: Integrated Taxonomic Information System
candidate_datasets.role: the taxonomic universe of insect orders against which published size samples can be matched

obstacles: Sexual size dimorphism is published in papers and supplements, with a bias toward a few orders.
No single open table covers insects that mate.
'Most' requires a sampling frame and a phylogenetic weighting.
rationale: Female-larger and male-larger insects are both well measured in scattered datasets, so a partial comparative test can be assembled. Those samples do not constitute a downloadable census of mating insects. The majority claim is testable on studied orders and remains open as a statement about insects in general.

operationalization: Score, across insects that copulate, whether the female inserts a part into the male or the male inserts a part into the female. The claim holds if female insertion is the majority pattern.

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: copulatory-anatomy accounts for major insect orders

candidate_datasets.name: Integrated Taxonomic Information System
candidate_datasets.role: order-level frame for sampling genitalia descriptions

obstacles: Genital orientation is described in taxonomic papers and is not a cross-order table.
A few groups with a female intromittent organ do not settle 'most'.
Building a fair sample across orders is months of compilation.
rationale: Which sex inserts is a discrete anatomical fact and is described for enormous numbers of species. Existing syntheses cover orders well enough to inspect the pattern, and they are not a dataset from which a prevalence can be computed directly. The claim is partly testable and laborious at full scope.

operationalization: In multi-generation human pedigrees, score traits that are absent in the parents and present in a child and in a more remote ancestor. The claim holds if such skipping occurs, and fails if resemblance is confined to parents.

candidate_datasets.name: ClinVar
candidate_datasets.role: clinical assertions with inheritance patterns, including autosomal recessive conditions expressed in offspring of unaffected parents

obstacles: The woman of Elis and the Ethiopian story is an anecdote, not a dataset.
Skipping can be recessive inheritance, incomplete penetrance or coincidence, and the claim only requires that skipping happens.
Open pedigree detail is richer for clinical traits than for ordinary family resemblance.
rationale: Reappearance of ancestral traits after a gap is a standard pedigree pattern, and public clinical-genetic archives document recessive transmission of that form. A small team can treat those records as a test of whether resemblance can skip generations. The particular ancient anecdote is not recoverable, and the general claim is.

operationalization: Compare acquired parental injuries, such as amputations, with the corresponding body part in the offspring. The claim holds if offspring are not always mutilated in the parental way, and would fail only if acquired mutilation were reliably inherited.
obstacles: Acquired injury has to be separated from congenital malformation.
There is no single registry of parental trauma and offspring phenotype; the evidence is the breeding, surgical and experimental record.
The claim is a negative generalization and is decided by documented non-transmission.
rationale: Non-inheritance of acquired mutilations is documented across animal breeding, surgery and experimental amputations. A small team can assemble decisive cases from that published record without new observation. The absence of one dedicated dataset limits convenience and does not leave the question untestable.

operationalization: Ask whether semen and sperm contain contributions drawn from every parental organ, as pangenesis requires, or a germline genome plus accessory-gland secretions. The claim holds if semen is not a sample of all body parts.

candidate_datasets.name: ProteomeXchange
candidate_datasets.role: seminal-plasma and sperm protein datasets with tissue attributions

candidate_datasets.name: UniProt
candidate_datasets.role: proteins of semen and sperm, with tissue specificity

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus
candidate_datasets.role: sperm and testis expression datasets contrasted with other organs

obstacles: Public molecular datasets are dominated by humans and a few model animals.
A restatement in which the genome 'comes from the whole body' would change the claim.
Seminal plasma mixes several glands, which is still far short of every part.
rationale: Proteomic and expression archives identify the tissues that contribute to semen and show a haploid germline plus a short list of accessory glands. That composition decides a claim that semen is withdrawn from all parts of the body. One or a few well-studied species are enough, because the claim is universal.

operationalization: Regress offspring number, litter size, clutch size or fecundity, on adult body mass across animals. The claim holds if larger species have fewer young, as a general negative relationship.

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: adult body mass and litter or clutch size across vertebrates

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: mammal body mass and litter size

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: body length and fecundity for fishes, the high-fecundity end of the comparison

obstacles: The pattern is a correlation with exceptions, so 'have few' and 'have many' need a stated transform.
Phylogeny and offspring size both track fecundity.
Invertebrates outside fish and amniote tables are less evenly covered.
rationale: Body size and offspring number are core fields in open life-history databases for mammals, other amniotes and fishes. A standard comparative regression can be run in days to weeks and will confirm or refute a general inverse relationship. Remaining gaps are invertebrate coverage and the need to control phylogeny, which qualify the result and do not block the test.

operationalization: From human growth standards, compare stature gained from birth to about age five with stature gained from age five to adulthood, and with total postnatal gain. Either reading of 'half the height gained in the rest of life' can be accepted or rejected against those curves.

candidate_datasets.name: WHO Child Growth Standards
candidate_datasets.role: length and height by age from birth to five years

candidate_datasets.name: National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey
candidate_datasets.role: measured stature by age in a population sample, including children and adults

obstacles: The phrase can mean half of later growth or half of all lifetime growth, and both are computable.
Modern standards are cross-sectional and secular change shifts adult height.
The claim is about humans in general, and the open standards are modern populations.
rationale: Age-specific human stature is in public growth standards and in NHANES measurements. Computing the fraction of lifetime height gained by age five is a short analysis. Wording ambiguity and secular change affect the interpretation, and they are handled by reporting both readings on the same tables.

operationalization: Compare fertility, time to pregnancy or live births, across adiposity classes in women and men. The fertility clause holds if fatter people are less fertile; the concoction clause needs semen volume or menstrual loss to fall as fat stores rise.

candidate_datasets.name: National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey
candidate_datasets.role: body-mass index together with reproductive-history items for women and men

obstacles: Survey fertility items are coarse, and age, disease and low body weight confound a fat-versus-fertile contrast.
The diversion of secretion into fat is not measured by a fertility rate.
Clinical cohorts with semen analysis and adiposity exist as papers and are often access-restricted.
rationale: NHANES links body composition to reproductive history in an open sample, which can test whether higher adiposity goes with lower fertility. The design leaves serious confounds, and it does not contain the physiological diversion Aristotle proposes. The fertility association is partly testable; the mechanism is not in that survey.

operationalization: Compare the composition of semen with urine and with a glandular secretion that supplies nutrients to sperm. A nutritive secretion is supported if semen is rich in sperm nutrients from accessory glands; 'the last stage of nutriment' has no further chemical criterion.

candidate_datasets.name: UniProt
candidate_datasets.role: seminal proteins and their glandular origins

candidate_datasets.name: ProteomeXchange
candidate_datasets.role: seminal-plasma composition datasets

obstacles: 'Last stage of useful nutriment' is a concoction category.
A secretion that feeds sperm is compatible with more than one theoretical label.
Composition data are strong for humans and weak for animals at large.
rationale: Seminal biochemistry can show that semen is a glandular product containing sugars and proteins used by sperm, which bears on 'secretion' and on 'useful'. The same measurements do not isolate a final stage of nutriment or refute every rival description of a secretion. The claim is only partly turned into a test.

operationalization: Compare the age distribution of spermarche, voice change and first ejaculation in boys with the age of menarche and breast development in girls. The claim holds if those events fall in the same span of life.

candidate_datasets.name: National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey
candidate_datasets.role: age at menarche and adolescent development items

candidate_datasets.name: WHO Child Growth Standards
candidate_datasets.role: adolescent growth and pubertal reference context for the same ages

obstacles: Spermarche is poorly represented in the surveys that record menarche.
'The same time of life' allows a window of years rather than a shared birthday.
Secular trends differ by sex and population.
rationale: Age at menarche is a standard public variable, and male pubertal timing is available in a smaller published literature that can be set beside it. The two are not one harmonized open table. A restricted comparison of modern populations can test whether the events coincide in life stage.

operationalization: Compare female and male adult mass in viviparous mammals, and ask whether female-smaller dimorphism is confined to species that menstruate. The size clause holds if females are smaller in this class; the menstrual explanation holds only if non-menstruating viviparous species lack that dimorphism.

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: adult body mass and life history for viviparous mammals, as the species frame for a sex-size comparison

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: body-mass records for the same mammals, including monotremes and therians

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: accounts that state male and female size, and whether a species menstruates or has an estrous cycle

obstacles: Female-larger mammals are common, so the size clause is an empirical distribution rather than a definition.
Menstruation is known from few clades and is not a field in the mass tables.
Sexual selection predicts size dimorphism independently of menstrual loss.
rationale: Adult body mass for mammals is downloadable, and many species accounts give male and female sizes, so the claim that viviparous females are smaller can be tested for a large subset. Sex-specific mass is not a single column in the main life-history tables, and menstruation is a separate character known for few clades. The size pattern is therefore partly testable now, while the menstrual explanation needs a compilation those tables do not contain.

operationalization: The claim defines the female as an impotent male who cannot concoct the final nutriment into semen. Failure to produce semen is the definition being used, and it does not add a measurement that could come out against the claim.
obstacles: Inability to concoct semen is how this passage says what a female is.
Hormone, gamete and genetic comparisons become a different claim once 'impotent male' is redescribed.
rationale: The sentence is a definitional theory of sex. Females' lack of semen is the observation it builds in, so that observation cannot test it. Datasets of gametes and endocrinology would answer a reconstructed physiological hypothesis, not this wording.

operationalization: Score cyclic menstrual shedding across humans and viviparous quadrupeds, with the mule as the stated defective case, and compare the amount of discharge with that of women. The claim holds if all non-defective members of the class menstruate, in smaller quantity than women.

candidate_datasets.name: PanTHERIA
candidate_datasets.role: the species list of viviparous quadrupeds against which menstruation records can be joined

candidate_datasets.name: Animal Diversity Web
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive-cycle accounts distinguishing estrus, menstruation and pregnancy bleeding

candidate_datasets.name: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database
candidate_datasets.role: life-history coverage of the mammal groups in the claim, including equids and the mule's parents

obstacles: Menstruation has to mean cyclic endometrial shedding, kept distinct from estrus.
Abundance relative to women is qualitative in most accounts.
Horses do not menstruate, so the mule's sterility is not the only equid case.
rationale: Which mammals menstruate is a reviewed comparative fact, and the species frame of viviparous quadrupeds is in open mammal databases. Species accounts separate estrus from menstruation for the main orders. A small team can decide whether menstruation is general in the class and merely lighter than in women.

operationalization: Relate breast projection at first menses to a length of about two finger-breadths. The claim holds if menarche usually coincides with that degree of breast rise.

candidate_datasets.name: National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey
candidate_datasets.role: age at menarche and adolescent anthropometry, as a coarse public proxy for pubertal stage

obstacles: Two fingers' breadth is not a Tanner stage or a recorded breast measurement.
Cohorts that link breast stage to menarche are published and are not one open table.
Finger breadth varies with the observer.
rationale: Public surveys date menarche and record some adolescent body measures, which can place menarche in a stage of development. They do not record breast rise in finger-breadths. Pediatric studies come closer and still have to be compiled, so only a loose proxy of the timing claim is available.

operationalization: Ask whether any material from the male, genome, centriole or sperm proteins, becomes part of the embryo, or whether the male contributes only a motion and a form. The claim holds if normal embryos contain nothing material from the father.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Genome
candidate_datasets.role: reference genomes and parent-offspring genetic data showing paternal DNA in offspring

candidate_datasets.name: Ensembl
candidate_datasets.role: gene models and comparative genomics for the paternal contribution to the zygote

candidate_datasets.name: UniProt
candidate_datasets.role: sperm and zygote proteins, including paternal contributions retained in the embryo

obstacles: The wording 'need not' is modal; a normal requirement for paternal DNA answers it for actual animal generation.
Coverage is best for humans and model species, which is enough for a universal denial of male material.
Centrioles and proteins are material in a broader sense than DNA alone.
rationale: Parentage and genome databases show that offspring carry a paternal genome, which is material from the male inside the embryo. That result can be read off existing genetic resources without new experiments. It decides the claim that nothing material from the male need enter the offspring and that his role is only motion and form.

operationalization: Classify hens' eggs by stage at mating, ovarian or freshly ovulated yolk versus an oviductal egg that has albumen, and record which of those eggs hatch as fertile. The claim holds if a mating while the egg is still entirely yellow converts a wind-egg into a fertile egg.
obstacles: Fertilization timing in the hen is established in poultry physiology rather than a downloadable trial table.
Sperm-storage tubules fertilize later ovulations, which can resemble fertilization of an egg already under way.
Wind-egg means an unfertilized ovum, and farm records rarely time the mating to yolk color.
rationale: The timing of fertilization relative to albumen secretion is known in detail for the domestic fowl, so the yellow-versus-white criterion can be interpreted and checked against that physiology. The original observation, a particular mating converting a specified yolk, is not stored as a reusable dataset. The claim is testable from the published experimental record for the chicken and only by analogy for other birds.

operationalization: Assign paternity in clutches where a second cock mates while eggs are still yolk, and measure the share of chicks sired by the second male. The claim holds only if the whole brood resembles, and is sired by, the second cock.
obstacles: Sequential-mating trials in poultry exist as papers, not as a public database.
'The whole brood' is stricter than a statistical last-male advantage.
Plumage resemblance and genetic paternity can diverge.
rationale: Sperm competition and second-male paternity in chickens have been measured, so the all-or-none claim about a second cock can be compared with those results. The trials are scattered and small. They can refute or qualify 'the whole brood' for the fowl and do not constitute a standing dataset.

operationalization: Among externally fertilizing fishes, compare fertilization of eggs that sperm reach with eggs from the same spawning that sperm do not reach. The claim holds if only the contacted eggs are fertilized.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: fertilization mode, external versus internal, and reproductive guild for oviparous fishes

obstacles: FishBase codes the mode of fertilization and does not store egg-by-egg exposure trials.
Those trials are published for model and commercial teleosts.
Internally fertilizing oviparous fishes sit outside the milt-sprinkling description.
rationale: External fertilization, with sperm meeting eggs after laying, is a coded life-history field for a large share of fishes. Experimental embryology of teleosts records that unexposed eggs are not fertilized. Together the database and those studies decide the claim for the oviparous, externally fertilizing fishes it describes.

operationalization: Score gonochorism versus hermaphroditism in animals that locomote, and compare that with sessile animals. The claim holds if every motile species has separate male and female individuals.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: sexual system of fishes, including simultaneous and sequential hermaphroditism

candidate_datasets.name: SeaLifeBase
candidate_datasets.role: sexual systems of motile invertebrates such as gastropods, and of sessile groups for the contrast

candidate_datasets.name: World Register of Marine Species
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic frame for the motile and attached animals being compared

obstacles: Wrasses, hamlets, slugs and earthworms are motile hermaphrodites and are the deciding counterexamples if present.
Invertebrate sexual systems are less completely coded than those of fishes.
Separate sexes should be distinguished from the mere occurrence of sexual reproduction.
rationale: FishBase records hermaphroditism as a reproductive trait, and marine invertebrate compilations cover many motile hermaphrodites. A small team can list motile species that are not gonochoric and thereby confirm or refute the universal. Remaining uncertainty is coverage of terrestrial invertebrates, not the existence of a test.

operationalization: The claim says animals generate so that the kind can be eternal as a species, since the individual cannot be. That assigns a purpose to generation. Species durations and extinctions would test a different assertion, that species in fact last forever.
obstacles: 'Eternal as a species' is offered as the end for which generation exists.
